status.reason: The claim rests on one network meta-analysis whose six trial reports are unread. The review does not report each trial's direction (Table 1 marks only 'no significant difference'), so the METHODS §6.4 condition for counting pooled trials, that the review reports their direction, is not met. The trials test five different pairs; only aripiprazole vs risperidone has two trials, and their separate results are not given. A run of non-significant results in small head-to-head trials is not a replicated direction, and on an insufficient-evidence claim 'replicated' would tell readers that several teams found the same thing. The two Chinese trials also share investigators (G. Wang, W. Hao, M. C. Chawarski; reference list, p. 8). The network estimates come from one analysis, and both advantages over risperidone pass through one trial. The narrative reviews describe the same trials (the olanzapine–haloperidol and quetiapine–haloperidol trials), so they add no independent study.

status.reason: Persistence beyond a month ranges from 0% to 96%. The review's partial explanations (laboratory vs clinical designs; Japanese vs other studies) leave wide unexplained spread within groups (18–96% in Japan, 0–39% elsewhere), and later schizophrenia diagnoses run from 5% to about 39%. The inconsistency is in size, not in whether persistence occurs in clinical samples, and the statement already makes that clear.

grade.reason: Descriptive claim, start low; risk of bias −1 and inconsistency −1 are right, and imprecision (unweighted medians, no intervals) could be added without changing the floor. Two reasons need correcting. (1) The laboratory studies observed no persistence (symptoms resolved within 12 hours to 7 days); persistence was not impossible by design. (2) The Japanese studies did not mostly use ICD-10: the review gives ICD-10 for 35% and DSM-IV for 25% of them, against 6% and 42% elsewhere, so the diagnostic explanation covers about a third of them at most and is untested.

plain.reason: 1 in 4 (median 25%), from none to almost all (0–96%), 1 in 20 to 2 in 5 later diagnosed (5% to about 39%) and psychosis often returning with renewed use all match the statement, and the text disclaims causation.
